results.title: Residence in Finland for EU citizens: Migri and DVV | Hello Expat
results.author: The Hello Expat editorial team
highlights:
Only if you stay longer than three months. Up to three months you need nothing but a valid passport or identity card. The InfoFinland page on EU citizens specifies that the three months are counted from your last departure from Finland, not from the first time you ever visited.

Beyond three months, you apply to the Finnish Immigration Service (Maahanmuuttovirasto, Migri) to register your right of residence. The deadline, per InfoFinland, is three months from arrival. This applies to citizens of EU member states, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. Citizens of Denmark, Iceland, Norway and Sweden do not apply to Migri at all; they register their personal data at the DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency).

...

You need one of the following:

- you are an employee (a contract is enough proof);
- you are self-employed (trade register extracts, client contracts);
- you are a student (a certificate of attendance, not only an admission letter, and comprehensive health insurance);
- you are a family member of an EU citizen, or of a Finnish citizen under certain conditions;
- you have sufficient resources for yourself and your family, for example as a pensioner.

On resources, Migri sets no fixed amount. The test is that social assistance must not become your main support. Retirees should bring proof of comprehensive health insurance; the S1 form from the country paying your pension serves that purpose (see Kela in Finland).

Looking for work does not give you registration by itself. You may come to look for a job for a reasonable time, but registration needs a real ground.

## How do you register your right of residence with Migri?

The sequence on Migri's page runs as follows:

1. Apply in Enter Finland (the online service) or on a paper form. You must submit it yourself, although you can apply for your child.
2. Pay €53. In 2026 the fee is the same online and on paper. You can pay by card or Finnish online banking when you submit, or at the service point.
3. Book an appointment at a Migri service point to prove your identity. Bring your passport or identity card and the originals and copies of your attachments.
4. Wait for the decision. Migri may contact you for more information.
5. Collect the decision at the service point, in Enter Finland or by post. If approved, you may receive the EU registration certificate on the spot or later.

Documents that are not in Finnish, Swedish or English need an authorised translation, unless they come with the EU's multilingual standard form. You can appeal a refusal to the administrative court.

Not sure which paperwork applies to you?

Unsure which ground fits your situation, or what counts as enough resources? Moovy can look at your case, tell you which documents to bring to the Migri counter and draft a Finnish or Swedish message for the authority.

## What does Migri not ask you to wait for?

Work. An EU citizen may work from the day of arrival, even while the application is pending. What you cannot do is get registered early: as an employee, Migri registers you only once your employment has started; as a student, once your studies have started.

The other thing to avoid is treating the Migri certificate as the end. It proves your right to stay. It does not give you an address, a personal identity code or a place in the healthcare system. That is the DVV's job.

...

You fill in the DVV's online registration form, which needs no electronic identification, then book a visit and attend within one month of submitting, children included. Registration is free. Bring a valid passport or EU identity card, the Migri certificate, and proof of work or studies.

...

The Migri registration has no expiry date and is not renewed. After five years of continuous legal residence you can ask Migri to confirm permanent residence; the fee in 2026 is the same €53. If you lose your certificate, a copy is free when the registration is less than two years old, otherwise you pay for a new certificate (the fee listed is €50).

Remember that the three-month counter for visits restarts each time you return to Finland, so a long absence followed by a new stay is treated differently from a continuous residence. If you plan an extended absence, ask Migri before you leave.

## What should you prepare before registering your residence in Finland?

Preparation decides how fast you get through. Gather the originals of everything before you book the Migri appointment, because the officer checks them against your online attachments and you will not be able to email a missing page afterwards.

For an employee, that means the employment contract or another employer document showing the start date, salary and duties. For a student, a certificate of attendance and proof of comprehensive health insurance. For a self-employed person, trade register extracts or client contracts. For a pensioner, proof of health cover and proof of income. Anything not in Finnish, Swedish or English needs an authorised translation.

Plan the timing too. Migri publishes processing times on its website, and they change with the season; check them before you travel rather than relying on a figure from a forum. The cheap mistake is to apply on day one for a job that starts in two months. The expensive one is to apply on day ninety.

...

## Which mistakes slow people down?

Letting the three months run out is number one. Filing too early as an employee is number two: the application waits until your contract has begun. Number three is forgetting the DVV step. Number four is leaving family documents unlegalised: a certificate issued outside the Nordic countries and the EU generally needs legalisation before Finnish authorities accept it.

Do these in order and the Finnish system rewards you with something rare: it simply works.

results.title: How EU/EEA Citizens Register Their Right of Residence in Finland - Finland Handbook
results.author: Finland Handbook Editorial Team
highlights:
After you've submitted your application online, the next crucial step is to book an appointment at a Migri service point for identification. This is where you'll present your original documents, prove your identity, and sometimes provide biometrics (though for EU registration, it's mostly about verifying your identity and documents). You can find the nearest Migri service point on their website, usually in major cities like Helsinki, Tampere, Turku, or Oulu. Remember to book this appointment as soon as you submit your online application, because appointment slots, especially in busy periods, can fill up fast! This whole process of interacting with the system is covered in more detail in our guide on Dealing with Migri and Enter Finland: Applications, Waiting, and Decisions.

...

### Necessary Documentation: What to Prepare

Regardless of your basis for residence, having your documents organized is half the battle won. Here's a general checklist, but always refer to Migri's website for the most up-to-date and specific requirements for your situation.

- Valid Passport or National ID Card: Your primary form of identification. Make sure it hasn't expired!
- Online Application Form: This will be filled out via Enter Finland.
- Proof of Basis for Residence: As detailed above (e.g., employment contract, study certificate, bank statements).
- Health Insurance Certificate: If applicable to your category (especially for students and those with sufficient funds).
- Family Documents: If applying on the basis of family ties, bring original marriage certificates, birth certificates, etc. Remember, if these documents are not in Finnish, Swedish, or English, you must get them officially translated by an authorized translator. This is where services like Translayte or RushTranslate become indispensable, ensuring your documents meet the rigorous standards of Finnish bureaucracy. They understand the need for certified translations, which are usually required for official purposes like this.

Always bring the original documents to your Migri appointment. Photocopies are generally not enough, as they need to verify the authenticity.

1. Book Your Appointment: You'll typically be prompted to book an appointment at a Migri service point directly through the Enter Finland portal, or you'll be directed to a separate booking system. Choose a time and location that works for you. As mentioned before, book this promptly – waiting lists can be long, and you don't want to exceed your three-month registration window because you couldn't get an appointment.
2. Prepare for the Appointment: This is the most critical part for many. You must bring all the original documents that you uploaded online. This includes your valid passport or national ID card, your employment contract, university acceptance, family certificates, bank statements, and any health insurance certificates. If you used Translayte or RushTranslate for certified translations of documents, bring the original documents and their certified translations. The official at Migri will need to see and verify the originals against your application.

### Lost Documents or Unclear Status

One of the most common anxieties revolves around lost documents or simply feeling unsure about your status. What if you misplace your Certificate of an EU citizen's right of residence? Or what if you're not entirely sure if your initial application was processed correctly?

- Replacing Lost Documents: If you lose your paper Certificate of an EU citizen's right of residence, don't panic. Migri maintains records. You can contact them directly, explain your situation, and usually, they can provide you with a new printout or a verified copy. It might involve a small administrative fee, but it's generally a straightforward process.
- Unclear Status: If you're feeling unsure about whether your registration went through, or if you've been waiting an unusually long time, the first point of contact should always be Migri. You can check the status of your application on Enter Finland, but if that doesn't provide clarity, their customer service (phone or email) can often help. Be prepared to provide your application reference number or personal details. Sometimes, contacting local expat associations or municipal integration services can also offer guidance, as they often deal with similar queries from other newcomers. Remember, official translations of documents, particularly from countries where English, Swedish, or Finnish aren't official languages, are often a sticking point. Ensure that any documents from your home country, such as marriage certificates or academic degrees, were translated by a certified professional. Translayte and RushTranslate offer such services, which are critical for ensuring your documents are accepted without question by Migri or DVV.

results.title: Residence permit and official matters for new students - UEF Kamu
highlights:
### EU citizens and citizens of Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland

- You may enter Finland without a visa or residence permit
- If you stay longer than 3 months (90 days), you should 

- register your right of residence (opens in a new tab) with the Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) (opens in a new tab)
- The registration should be done within 3 months of arrival.
- If you travel outside the Finnish borders, you may stay another 90 days without the registration.

#### Registering your right of residcence

- Apply online (opens in a new tab)
- Visit a Migri service point (opens in a new tab) to verify your identity and present original documents. Contact information (opens in a new tab) for Migri offices.
- Book an appointment well in advance.
- The closest Migri office is in Kuopio.
- Bring original documents to Migri.
- If the documents are not in Finnish, Swedish or English, they must be translated by an authorised translator.
- Registration is subject to a processing fee.
